final_message:
All three versions are complete and pass every sample byte-exactly.

**Algorithm (all versions):** Dijkstra per source, specialized for integer weights 1..1000. Statistics (reachable count, distance sum, farthest distance with smallest-node tiebreak) are accumulated as each node is settled in increasing distance order. Self-loops are skipped, since they can never shorten a path.

**Rust — [rust/src/main.rs](/D:/projects/nb-work/39-rust-vs-python/sessions/wonder/routes/rust/src/main.rs):**
Hand-written fast byte-level integer parser over `fs::read`, CSR adjacency (`u32` neighbours, `u16` weights), and Dial's algorithm with a circular bucket array of size `max_weight+1`. An occupancy bitmask (16×`u64`) jumps directly to the next non-empty bucket, so cost is O(N+M) per source regardless of the largest distance. Distances are `u64`. Release profile in [rust/Cargo.toml](/D:/projects/nb-work/39-rust-vs-python/sessions/wonder/routes/rust/Cargo.toml) uses fat LTO, one codegen unit, and `panic="abort"`. Single-threaded, no crates used at runtime.

**Python plain — [plain.py](/D:/projects/nb-work/39-rust-vs-python/sessions/wonder/routes/plain.py):**
Standard library only. Parses with `list(map(int, data.split()))`, builds adjacency as lists of packed ints (`neighbour << 10 | weight`), and runs the same Dial algorithm in pure Python: bucket lists, a `bytearray` visited set, and a Python-int occupancy bitmask (via lowest-set-bit extraction) to skip empty buckets. Output is written through `sys.stdout.buffer` so line endings are LF on Windows, matching the samples.

**Python fast — [fast.py](/D:/projects/nb-work/39-rust-vs-python/sessions/wonder/routes/fast.py):**
Vectorized Δ-stepping (Δ=256) with NumPy: edges are relaxed in bulk from whole frontier sets (CSR built with `argsort`/`bincount`/`cumsum`, per-destination minima via `np.minimum.at`), light edges iterated to closure within a bucket, heavy edges relaxed once per settled bucket, and future buckets tracked in a small heap. Parsing uses `map(int, ...)` into a NumPy array because `np.fromstring(sep=...)` measured ~3× slower on the large input. Very sparse, chain-like graphs (fewer than 2 edges per node) fall back to the plain Dial loop, where NumPy's per-step overhead would dominate.

**Verification:**
- Samples: s1, s2, s3 — plain PASS, fast PASS, rust PASS (byte-exact against the `*.out` files).
- 60 randomized small graphs (disconnected nodes, self-loops, parallel edges, tie cases) checked against an independent `heapq` reference: all three versions agree on every trial; a dense chain graph exercising the Δ-stepping path with FAR ≈ 2,000,000 and a single isolated node also agree.
- On a synthetic benchmark-size input (N=300,000, M=900,000, Q=6, all outputs agreeing): Rust ≈ 0.4 s, fast.py ≈ 4.5 s, plain.py ≈ 11 s.

request.prompt:
You are writing three versions of the same program, one in Rust and two in Python, for a comparison of how
fast and how memory-hungry each version is.

The task is described in SPEC.md in this folder. The folder samples/ holds example inputs (`*.in`), each with
the exact expected output (`*.out`).

Write these three files:

1. `rust/src/main.rs`: Rust, compiled with rustc 1.99 (edition 2024). The Cargo project in `rust/` is set
   up. The only crates you may use are serde (with derive), serde_json, regex and rayon. They are already
   listed in `rust/Cargo.toml` and vendored, so build offline with `cargo build --release --offline` inside
   `rust/`. Do not add other dependencies. You may change the `[profile.release]` settings in
   `rust/Cargo.toml`.
2. `plain.py`: Python 3.13, standard library only.
3. `fast.py`: Python 3.13, standard library plus NumPy 2.2.

Each program is run with the path of one input file as its argument (SPEC.md says if a task takes more
arguments). It reads that file and writes the answer to standard output exactly as SPEC.md describes. The
Python versions are run as `C:\Python313\python.exe plain.py INPUT_PATH` and
`C:\Python313\python.exe fast.py INPUT_PATH`, and the Rust version as the release binary
`rust/target/release/solution.exe INPUT_PATH`.

Your goals, in order:

1. Every version must print the correct output for any valid input as SPEC.md defines it, not only for the
   samples.
2. Make each version as fast as you can. Write each one the way a skilled developer in that language would
   write fast code, using that language's own strengths.

Use a single thread and a single process unless SPEC.md says otherwise. Do not precompute or embed answers,
start other programs, or read any file other than the input.

The programs will be run on Windows 11 on a 16-core laptop, on larger inputs of the same kind; SPEC.md gives
the benchmark size. Test all three versions against every sample before you finish. Work only inside this
folder, and take at most about 45 minutes. Other programs run on this machine at the same time:
never stop a process you did not start yourself, so do not kill processes by name (for example
`taskkill /IM python.exe` or `Stop-Process -Name python`); stop only your own processes, by process ID.

When you are done, reply with a short summary: the algorithm, the main choices you made for speed in each
version, and which samples each version passes.
